source_excerpt: We justify $\frac{\dd}{\dd\tau}\int F\dd x=\int\partial_\tau F\dd x\ge\int\Delta_xF\dd x=0$ on a compact interval $\tau\in[\tau_0,\tau_1]\subset(0,\infty)$. There $f_i(\tau,y)\le2m\norm{h_i}_\infty\sup_{\abs z\le m}g_\tau(y-z)\le Ce^{-y^2/(16\tau_1)}$ (for $\abs y\ge2m$ use $\abs{y-z}\ge\abs y/2$), and $\partial_y\log f_i$ is the average of $-(y-z)/(2\tau)$ over $z\in[-m,m]$ against a probability measure, so $\abs{\partial_y\log f_i(\tau,y)}\le(\abs y+m)/(2\tau_0)$; similar bounds hold for the second derivative. Using $\sum_ic_i(u_i\cdot x)^2=\abs x^2$, the functions $F$, $\partial_\tau F$ and the first two $x$-derivatives of $F$ are bounded by $C(1+\abs x^4)e^{-\abs x^2/(16\tau_1)}$ uniformly in $\tau\in[\tau_0,\tau_1]$. This justifies differentiating under the integral sign and shows $\int\Delta_xF\dd x=0$. Thus $\int F(\tau,x)\dd x$ is nondecreasing in $\tau$.
